questions.explanation: Both statements are true. Plotting 1/V against 1/[S] (the double-reciprocal transform) turns the Michaelis-Menten hyperbola into a straight line, from which Km and Vmax can be read directly from the slope and intercepts — a correct explanation.

questions.stem: The major macromolecules that are usually studied in biochemistry include
questions.explanation: All three — proteins, nucleic acids, and carbohydrates (plus lipids) — are the major classes of biomolecules central to biochemistry.

questions.stem: Which of the following is/are TRUE about Proteins?
items: Basic functional units are amino acids.
There are three levels of structure in Proteins.
Amino acid sequences in proteins are stabilized by carbon bonding.
questions.explanation: Statement I is true (amino acids are the building blocks). Statement II is true in the sense intended here (primary, secondary, tertiary — quaternary applies only to multi-subunit proteins). Statement III is false: the primary sequence is held together by peptide (amide) bonds, not 'carbon bonding'.

questions.stem: Metabolism is important because
items: It allows the transformation of energy
Energy is produced solely for cell repair
questions.explanation: Metabolism does allow transformation and interconversion of energy (I) and it does generate/consume intermediates that link pathways together (II, as understood here). Statement III is false — energy produced from metabolism is used for many purposes (movement, biosynthesis, transport, thermoregulation), not solely for cell repair.

questions.stem: In predicting spontaneity of reactions, if ΔG is negative and large, the reaction is
questions.explanation: A large negative ΔG means the reaction releases free energy (exergonic, I) and will proceed spontaneously (II). Statement III is considered not an automatic consequence purely of the sign/magnitude of ΔG in the way the other two are, hence it is excluded here.

questions.stem: Which of the following is/are the common monosaccharide(s)?
questions.explanation: Glucose and fructose are monosaccharides (simple sugars). Cellulose is a polysaccharide (a polymer of glucose units), not a monosaccharide, so statement I is false.

questions.stem: In metabolism
items: Substrates are transformed to products via non-specific intermediates.
questions.explanation: Metabolism is highly coordinated (I) and consists of many interconnected pathways (II). Statement III is false — intermediates in metabolic pathways are generally highly SPECIFIC, not non-specific, which is part of what allows tight regulation.

questions.stem: Characteristics of enzymes include(s)
items: the acceleration in the rate of breaking of bonds.
questions.explanation: All three are core enzyme characteristics: high specificity for substrates, loss of activity on denaturation (loss of 3D structure), and acceleration of bond-breaking/making steps of a reaction.

questions.stem: Classes of enzymes include (s)
questions.explanation: Ligases and transferases are genuine enzyme class names. 'Hydrolysis' is the name of a type of reaction, not an enzyme class — the correct class name is 'hydrolase'. Because statement I uses the wrong term, it is excluded.

questions.stem: Biological functions of enzymes include(s)
questions.explanation: Enzymes are central to digestion (I) and cellular regulation (II, e.g. controlling metabolic flux). Signal transduction (III) is driven mainly by receptors, kinases acting as signalling relays and second messengers rather than being classed as a core 'enzyme function' in this scheme, so it is excluded here.

questions.stem: The protein part of the enzyme is called
questions.explanation: The apoenzyme is, by definition, the protein-only part of an enzyme before it binds its cofactor/coenzyme. The holoenzyme is apoenzyme + cofactor together (not just the protein part), and a zymogen is an inactive enzyme precursor — neither matches the definition asked for.

questions.stem: Classes of enzymes include (s)
questions.explanation: Unlike Q20, all three terms here are correctly named: hydrolases, ligases and transferases are three of the standard six/seven major enzyme classes (alongside oxidoreductases, lyases and isomerases).

questions.stem: Most of the members of vitamin B complex act as
questions.explanation: I and II are both true. The B vitamins are the classic COENZYME precursors — niacin → NAD⁺, riboflavin → FAD, thiamine → TPP, pantothenate → coenzyme A — and a coenzyme is simply an organic cofactor. Only III is false: a holoenzyme is the whole active complex.

questions.stem: Enzymes exhibit specificity based on
questions.explanation: In this scheme, shape (the classic 'lock and key' complementarity) is highlighted as the key basis of specificity (I only) tested here, rather than charge or size individually.

questions.stem: The following are way(s) by which enzymes are regulated
questions.explanation: Cells regulate enzyme activity by controlling how much enzyme is produced (I) and via inhibitors/activators (II). Temperature (III) is an external physical condition that affects enzyme activity but is not a physiological 'regulation' mechanism the cell uses deliberately, so it's excluded.

questions.stem: Enzymes involved in inhibition is/are known as
questions.explanation: Inhibitors (II) directly block enzyme activity, and many regulatory enzymes that respond to inhibitors are allosteric enzymes (III). 'Holoenzyme' (I) simply refers to a complete enzyme with its cofactor — unrelated to inhibition — so it is excluded.

questions.stem: Which of the following is/are substrate-specific enzyme?
questions.explanation: Lactase acts on one specific substrate, lactose, making it strictly substrate-specific (I only). Hexokinase and glucokinase, by contrast, can act on more than one hexose sugar (hexokinase especially is broadly specific for hexoses), so they are not considered strictly substrate-specific here.

questions.stem: Which of the following influence feedback inhibition?
questions.explanation: Feedback inhibition is, by definition, driven by the accumulation of the pathway's END PRODUCT, which binds back to an earlier enzyme (often allosterically) to slow the pathway (I only). Temperature and pH affect enzyme activity generally, but they are not what defines feedback inhibition.

questions.stem: Cofactors
questions.explanation: II and III are both correct definitions. A cofactor bound loosely and reversibly is a COENZYME (NAD⁺, FAD, coenzyme A); one bound tightly, often covalently, is a PROSTHETIC GROUP (haem, biotin). Only I is false — cofactors span inorganic metal ions and organic molecules alike.

questions.stem: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is an allosteric regulator of glycolysis and gluconeogenesis
questions.reason: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activates Fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase and inhibits phosphofructokinase 1.

options.label: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE

questions.explanation: The assertion is true but the reason has it backwards. Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate ACTIVATES phosphofructokinase-1 and INHIBITS fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase — the switch that favours glycolysis in the fed state and gluconeogenesis in the fasted state.

questions.stem: ATP is an allosteric inhibitor of gluconeogenesis
questions.reason: ATP inhibits the conversion of Fructose-6-phosphate to Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate by phosphofructokinase 1.

options.label: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE

questions.explanation: The ASSERTION is false and the REASON is true. ATP does not inhibit gluconeogenesis — high ATP signals plenty of energy, which SHUTS DOWN glycolysis and permits gluconeogenesis. The reason describes the real effect correctly: ATP allosterically inhibits phosphofructokinase-1, the enzyme converting fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate — a glycolytic step, not a gluconeogenic one.

questions.stem: Gluconeogenesis and glycolysis are considered opposing pathways
questions.reason: Gluconeogenesis is a direct reversal of glycolysis.

options.label: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE

questions.explanation: The assertion is true but the reason is false. Gluconeogenesis is NOT a direct reversal of glycolysis. Three glycolytic steps are irreversible — hexokinase/glucokinase, phosphofructokinase-1 and pyruvate kinase — and gluconeogenesis bypasses them with four different enzymes: pyruvate carboxylase and PEP carboxykinase, then fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase. The other seven steps are the shared reversible ones.

questions.stem: Glucagon secretion favours gluconeogenesis
questions.reason: Glucagon secretion leads to phosphorylation of phosphofructokinase 2, which reduces the production of an inhibitor in gluconeogenesis.

options.label: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE

questions.explanation: Both statements are true and connected: glucagon activates PKA, which phosphorylates the bifunctional PFK-2/FBPase-2 enzyme. This inactivates its kinase domain (less F2,6BP made) and activates its phosphatase domain — lowering F2,6BP, an inhibitor of the gluconeogenic enzyme fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase — thereby favouring gluconeogenesis.

questions.section: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism
questions.stem: Gluconeogenesis is important in the following tissues:
questions.explanation: Gluconeogenesis is physiologically important FOR maintaining glucose supply to obligate glucose-dependent tissues — erythrocytes (which lack mitochondria and rely almost entirely on glycolysis) and the brain (which strongly prefers glucose). Hepatocytes are where gluconeogenesis actually takes place, but the liver itself is not the primary 'beneficiary' of the glucose it exports.

questions.section: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism
questions.stem: Enzymes involved in the regulation of gluconeogenesis include:
questions.explanation: Pyruvate carboxylase and fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase are key regulatory/rate-limiting enzymes unique to gluconeogenesis. Malate dehydrogenase catalyses a freely reversible step (used in the malate–aspartate shuttle) and is not considered a regulatory control point of the pathway.

questions.section: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism
questions.stem: In allosteric regulation of gluconeogenesis:
items: high levels of citrate increases the activity of fructose 1, 6 bisphosphatase
high levels of acetyl CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase
decreased levels of fructose 1, 6 bisphosphate reduces the activity of pyruvate kinase.
questions.explanation: All three are correct: citrate activates fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (while inhibiting PFK-1), acetyl-CoA is a classic allosteric activator of pyruvate carboxylase, and low fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (a feed-forward activator of pyruvate kinase) means less activation of pyruvate kinase.

questions.section: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism
questions.stem: Hormonal control of gluconeogenesis:
items: Insulin inhibits lipolysis which in turn inhibits gluconeogenesis
Glucagon decreases [fructose 2, 6 bisphosphate] thus enhancing gluconeogenesis.
questions.explanation: All three are true. I: a rising glucagon:insulin ratio is the fasting signal that switches gluconeogenesis on. II: insulin inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase, so lipolysis stops — that cuts the supply of glycerol (a gluconeogenic substrate) and of fatty acids, whose β-oxidation supplies the acetyl-CoA that allosterically ACTIVATES pyruvate carboxylase and the ATP that drives the pathway. Less lipolysis therefore means less gluconeogenesis. III: glucagon raises cAMP, PKA phosphorylates the bifunctional PFK-2/FBPase-2 enzyme, which switches it to its phosphatase mode; fructose-2,6-bisphosphate falls, which relieves the inhibition of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and removes the stimulation of PFK-1 — so gluconeogenesis is enhanced.

questions.section: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism
questions.stem: Glucagon induces the synthesis of the following enzymes:
questions.explanation: Glucagon (via cAMP/gene transcription) induces synthesis of the key gluconeogenic enzymes fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and PEP carboxykinase. It does NOT induce phosphofructokinase-1 — PFK-1 is a glycolytic enzyme, and glucagon acts to suppress, not promote, glycolysis.

questions.section: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism
questions.stem: Glycerol enters the pathway to glucose production as:
questions.explanation: Glycerol is phosphorylated (glycerol kinase) and oxidized to dihydroxyacetone phosphate, feeding into the gluconeogenic pathway upstream of the triose-phosphate stage — placing its entry conceptually alongside the earlier 3-carbon intermediates rather than at the pyruvate/PEP end of the pathway (III is excluded).

questions.section: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism
questions.stem: In Gluconeogenesis:
items: fructose 1,6 bisphosphatase is inhibited by an increased [AMP]
ingestion of uncooked eggs inhibits the conversion of pyruvate to PEP.
questions.explanation: All three are true. AMP inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase; citrate inhibits PFK-1; and raw egg white contains AVIDIN, which binds biotin, so pyruvate carboxylase cannot convert pyruvate to oxaloacetate.

questions.section: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism
questions.stem: During gluconeogenesis, the three irreversible steps of glycolysis have to be bypassed. The first step is the conversion of pyruvate to phosphoenolpyruvate. Which of the following statement is FALSE regarding the reaction step?
items: This reaction involves a two-step process catalyzed by pyruvate carboxylase and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase
Conversion of oxaloacetate from pyruvate occurs in the cytosol.
Formation of phosphoenolpyruvate requires only ATP as an energy source.
questions.explanation: Read the stem carefully — it asks which statements are FALSE. II and III are the false ones. II is false because pyruvate → oxaloacetate is catalysed by PYRUVATE CARBOXYLASE, a MITOCHONDRIAL enzyme, so it happens inside the mitochondrion, not the cytosol. III is false because the bypass does not run on ATP alone: pyruvate carboxylase spends ATP, but PEP carboxykinase then spends GTP. I is TRUE — it correctly describes the two-step bypass by pyruvate carboxylase and PEP carboxykinase — so it is not one of the false statements.

questions.section: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism
questions.stem: Step(s) in the payoff phase of glycolysis
items: Reversible conversion of dihydroxyacetone phosphate to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate
questions.explanation: PEP → pyruvate and G3P oxidation → 1,3-BPG are both substrate-level phosphorylation/oxidation steps that occur in the payoff (energy-generating) phase. The DHAP ↔ G3P isomerisation (triose phosphate isomerase) happens immediately after aldolase cleavage and is considered part of the earlier preparatory (investment) phase, not the payoff phase.

questions.section: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism
questions.stem: Intermediate(s) involved in substrate level phosphorylation in glycolysis
questions.explanation: 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate and phosphoenolpyruvate are the two high-energy intermediates that directly donate a phosphate group to ADP (substrate-level phosphorylation), generating ATP. 2-phosphoglycerate is only an intermediate of the enolase/mutase steps and does not itself donate a phosphate to ADP.

questions.section: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism
questions.stem: Which of the following enzymes participate in the 1st phase of glycolysis?
questions.explanation: Phosphoglucose isomerase (glucose-6-P → fructose-6-P) acts in the preparatory (1st) phase of glycolysis. Enolase and phosphoglycerate mutase act later, in the payoff phase — so only statement III belongs to the 1st phase.

questions.section: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism
questions.stem: The pathways for glucose converted from galactose include
questions.explanation: Once galactose is converted (via the Leloir pathway) to glucose-6-phosphate, that G6P can be used in glycolysis for energy or in glycogenesis for storage. It is not classified as entering 'gluconeogenesis', since gluconeogenesis specifically refers to synthesising new glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors.

questions.section: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism
questions.stem: Cataract due to galactokinase deficiency arises from
questions.explanation: With galactokinase deficiency, excess galactose is instead reduced by ALDOSE REDUCTASE (which is normally, not poorly, active) to galactitol. Galactitol accumulates in the lens (I), drawing water in osmotically and making the lens cells swell/permeable (II) — this is what causes the cataract. Statement III is false; it is not low aldose reductase activity that causes this — the enzyme is active enough to generate the damaging galactitol.

questions.section: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism
questions.stem: Galactosemia is
questions.explanation: Correction: Classic galactosemia is caused by deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT) — galactokinase deficiency causes a separate, milder disorder — so statement I is not accurate for 'galactosemia' as classically defined. Statement II is factually incorrect: galactosemia is inherited in an AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE pattern, not sex-linked. Only statement III is correct — it is a congenital disorder that presents in infancy. (This answer has been corrected from the original paper, which had marked 'A'.)

questions.section: Multiple Completion — Gluconeogenesis, Glycolysis & Galactose Metabolism
questions.stem: Galactose is produced from
questions.explanation: While galactose is structurally found in glycolipids and glycoproteins, the major dietary/exogenous SOURCE of galactose is lactose in milk (which is hydrolysed to glucose + galactose), making milk the key answer intended here.

questions.section: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option
questions.stem: Polyol pathway

options.text: Pathway is present in the liver
Pathway is not related to glucose concentration

questions.explanation: In the polyol pathway, aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol, and sorbitol dehydrogenase then converts sorbitol to fructose — so it does involve sorbitol dehydrogenase. Aldolase B belongs to fructose metabolism, not the polyol pathway; the pathway is most active in tissues like the lens, retina, nerve and kidney (not primarily the liver); and its flux rises with high glucose concentration (e.g. in hyperglycaemia), so it is very much related to glucose levels.

questions.section: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option
questions.stem: Which of the following is true about Essential fructosuria

options.text: Fructose is trapped within the cells
Caused by deficiency in hepatic fructokinase
A child from carrier parents has 50% chance of having this condition

questions.explanation: Essential fructosuria results from a deficiency of hepatic fructokinase, so ingested fructose cannot be phosphorylated in the liver and simply spills into the urine unchanged. It is a benign, largely ASYMPTOMATIC condition, and — being autosomal recessive — two carrier parents have a 25% (not 50%) chance of an affected child.

questions.section: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option
questions.stem: In hereditary fructose intolerance
questions.explanation: Hereditary fructose intolerance is caused by aldolase B deficiency. Fructose-1-phosphate cannot be cleaved further and accumulates, trapping cellular phosphate and secondarily inhibiting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis — leading to HYPOglycaemia (not hyperglycaemia) after fructose ingestion.

questions.section: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option
questions.stem: Aldose reductase is NOT found in the
questions.explanation: Aldose reductase (the first enzyme of the polyol pathway) is present in tissues such as the retina, nerve tissue, kidney, lens and erythrocytes. The liver has comparatively negligible aldose reductase activity, making it the correct 'NOT found in' answer.

questions.section: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option
questions.stem: How many enzymes are involved in the conversion of galactose to glucose?
questions.explanation: The Leloir pathway uses galactokinase, galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT), and UDP-galactose-4-epimerase, plus phosphoglucomutase to convert the resulting glucose-1-phosphate to glucose-6-phosphate — four enzymes in total in the standard teaching scheme.

questions.section: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option
questions.stem: Which enzyme phosphorylates fructose to fructose-6-phosphate
questions.explanation: In extrahepatic tissues (muscle, adipose), broadly-specific hexokinase phosphorylates fructose directly to fructose-6-phosphate. This is distinct from the LIVER pathway, where fructokinase instead produces fructose-1-phosphate — a classic distinction question.

questions.section: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option
questions.stem: Transporter involved in shuttling fructose into intestinal cells
questions.explanation: GLUT5 is the fructose-specific transporter located on the apical (luminal) membrane of intestinal enterocytes, mediating fructose absorption from the gut lumen.

questions.section: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option
questions.stem: Which of the following statements are true for fructolysis and glycolysis?

options.text: These processes share same intermediate structures
Leads to same metabolic fates for fructose and glucose
Rate of fructose and glucose transport is virtually the same
Both fructose and glucose are exclusively metabolized in the liver

questions.explanation: Fructolysis converges with glycolysis at the level of the triose phosphates (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate / dihydroxyacetone phosphate), so the two pathways do share common intermediate structures. Their regulation and tissue fates differ, transport uses different carriers (GLUT5 vs GLUT2/GLUT4) at different rates, and glucose is metabolised in virtually every tissue, not just the liver.

questions.section: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option
questions.stem: Fructose

options.text: In its free form is absorbed directly by intestines
Uptake occurs along a concentration gradient

questions.explanation: Dietary fructose (both free, and bound in sucrose) is estimated to make up roughly a fifth of typical carbohydrate/caloric intake in many modern diets. Fructose is not found only in the free form (it is also part of sucrose), and its intestinal absorption depends on the GLUT5 transporter rather than being unassisted.

questions.section: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option
questions.stem: Fructose is
questions.explanation: Fructose is a ketose — a polyhydroxyketone — whereas glucose is an aldose (a polyhydroxyaldehyde). They are structural isomers of one another, not epimers (epimers differ at a single stereocentre while retaining the same functional-group type).

questions.section: Fructose & Galactose Metabolism — Best Single Option
questions.stem: Which of the following clinical symptoms of classical galactosemia is a direct result of the accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate?
questions.explanation: Accumulated galactose-1-phosphate is directly hepatotoxic, damaging liver cells and causing jaundice. (By contrast, the cataracts of galactosemia are attributed to galactitol, formed via aldose reductase, rather than to galactose-1-phosphate itself.)

questions.stem: The Leloir pathway serves as the principal route for galactose metabolism
questions.reason: it converts galactose into glucose-1-phosphate, which can then enter glycolysis or glycogenesis.

questions.explanation: Both statements are true, and the reason correctly explains the assertion: the Leloir pathway (galactokinase, GALT, epimerase) is indeed the main way the body converts galactose into a usable glucose derivative.

questions.stem: Gluconeogenesis occurs mainly in the liver
questions.reason: gluconeogenesis helps to maintain glucose levels in the blood.

options.label: Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Assertion and Reason are both TRUE, but the Reason does NOT correctly explain the Assertion
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE
The Assertion is FALSE, but the Reason is TRUE
Both the Assertion and the Reason are FALSE

questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but the reason explains WHY gluconeogenesis matters generally, not WHY the liver specifically is the main site (that's because the liver -- and to a lesser extent the kidney cortex -- has the full enzyme set: pyruvate carboxylase, PEP carboxykinase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, and glucose-6-phosphatase).

questions.stem: Damage to the red blood cells of an individual with G6PD deficiency can be reduced by adequate activity of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Glutathione peroxidase uses reduced glutathione (GSH) to detoxify peroxides and protect the red cell membrane from oxidative damage.
